content: The base field border uses `--color-rule` (#e5e3e1) on a white sheet: about 1.2:1 contrast, far below the 3:1 that WCAG 1.4.11 requires to identify a control boundary. The border only becomes visible on hover/focus, so an unfocused field is nearly indistinguishable from the page and users with low vision cannot see where to type. Use a token that reaches 3:1 (the existing `--color-ink-3` #736d69 is ~4.6:1, or add a dedicated `--color-rule-input` around #8c8681 for a softer look) so the boundary is identifiable at rest.

`touch-action: none` disables *all* browser touch gestures on the sheet host — panning and pinch-zoom included — which directly contradicts the comment above it ("il browser può ancora fare pan, ma non zoomare il documento"). The JS in UniverSheet.tsx only intercepts two-finger pinch (touchstart/touchmove with `touches.length === 2`); single-finger panning and page scrolling over the sheet are then handled by nobody, so on a phone a tall sheet cannot be scrolled and the surrounding modal cannot be scrolled by dragging over the sheet. Blocking pinch-zoom also removes the browser zoom escape hatch (WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10). Use `touch-action: pan-x pan-y` (or `manipulation`) so native pan stays available while the pinch handler keeps controlling the sheet zoom.
suggestion_code:
touch-action: pan-x pan-y;
    overscroll-behavior: contain;

content: `display: none` removes the page name and the shortcut keys from the accessibility tree entirely, which contradicts the comment right above ("Le parole tolte restano ai lettori di schermo e nel titolo al passaggio") and the technique used for steps 3–5 in the very next rule. Screen-reader users lose the current page name and every keyboard hint as soon as the bar tightens. Use the same visually-hidden pattern (`position: absolute; width/height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%)`) instead of `display: none`.

`@keyframes reveal` is never referenced anywhere in the file (no `animation: reveal ...`), and the reduced-motion block still disables an animation on `main .mod` that this stylesheet never sets. Either the rule that applied `reveal` was dropped (in which case the documented "moduli visibili subito / rivelazione allo scorrimento" behaviour silently disappeared) or both the keyframes and the reduced-motion override are stale. Remove the dead keyframes, or re-attach them to the selector that was meant to use them, so the intent in the comments matches the code.

No code in `frontend/src` ever sets `data-closing`, so `:not([data-closing])` is always true and the guard is dead. Together with the unused `unfold`/`fold` keyframes below (never referenced by any `animation`), this looks like the closing animation of the menu was removed without cleaning up its hooks. Either wire the attribute/keyframes up or drop them, so a future reader does not assume a closing transition exists.

This whole `jss_*` skin targets Jspreadsheet CE, which is no longer a dependency (`frontend/package.json` only declares Univer) and no component in `frontend/src` renders a `tabularium-sheet` container. Keeping ~55 lines of library-specific overrides that can never match adds noise and, worse, suggests the sheet is still Jspreadsheet-based when `UniverSheet.tsx` is what actually renders the grid. Remove the block (the roadmap note in docs/spec/80-roadmap.md already records the migration) or keep it only if a Jspreadsheet-based surface still exists somewhere outside `frontend/src`.

Setting the standard `scrollbar-color`/`scrollbar-width` makes Chrome/Edge (121+) ignore the `::-webkit-scrollbar*` rules below, so the intended 10px track, the `--color-fill` groove and the `::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover` affordance never apply in the primary target browser; only Firefox gets the standard colouring and WebKit-based browsers get the custom scrollbar. Pick one approach — e.g. keep the standard properties and express the hover state with `scrollbar-color` on `:hover`, or drop the standard ones so the webkit rules stay authoritative.

Making the *default* state invisible means the content is only visible if a listener installed in `main.tsx` happens to run and if the `load`/`error` event is caught. Any path where that listener is absent (unit tests with jsdom, a different entry point, a component rendered before the listener, an `` whose `data-fade` attribute is added after the image already completed) leaves the image permanently blank — an invisible failure mode for real thumbnails. Prefer a fail-visible default: e.g. fade only when JS has marked the element as pending (`img[data-fade][data-pending] { opacity: 0 }`) or add an `animation` with a short `forwards` fallback, so a missing `data-loaded` degrades to "shown" instead of "hidden".

These two rules can never be observed: in `UniverSheet.tsx` the same callback sets `setReady(true)` and `setSkeletonGone(true)`, so the skeleton is unmounted in the same render that adds `data-ready` — there is no element left to transition, and the documented "sfuma in fretta" never happens. Additionally the rule depends on a sibling relationship that only holds for that one component. Either keep the skeleton mounted and let this CSS do the fade (which is what the comment promises) or delete the dead `transition`/sibling rule.

The body contains only an empty `#root`, so any failure in the bootstrap chain (module 404, syntax error in `main.tsx`, unsupported browser, JS disabled) leaves the user with a completely blank white page and no explanation. Add a `<noscript>` notice and a minimal in-page error affordance (e.g. `window.addEventListener('error')`/`unhandledrejection` written into `#root`) so a broken deploy is diagnosable instead of silent.

The head declares a light `color-scheme` but ships no `theme-color`, no `description` and no favicon link, so the browser issues a request for `/favicon.ico` on every load (404 noise in logs, and another URL that breaks under a non-root `BASE_PATH`). The DESIGN note claims the build is "finished"; the head should reflect that.

content: `testpaths` silently narrows default collection to `tests/`, which now duplicates the hard-coded target used by `scripts/check.sh` and both CI jobs (`python -m pytest tests -q`). Two independent sources of truth risk drift: if test code is ever added outside `tests/` (e.g. `scripts/cloud/test_cloud_connection.py` already matches the `test_*.py` pattern) or the CI argument changes, the suite will report success while a whole tree is never collected. Consider keeping `testpaths` as the single source of truth (list every test root explicitly) and dropping the redundant path argument from CI, so coverage of new test locations cannot be lost unnoticed.

`npm run build` uses `tsc -b`, which will also build the referenced project. `tsconfig.node.json` sets `composite: true` but neither `noEmit` nor an `outDir`, so the build emits `vite.config.js` / `vite.config.d.ts` next to the source. That pollutes the working tree and is dangerous here, because a generated `vite.config.js` in the same directory can be picked up by Vite instead of `vite.config.ts` on subsequent runs. Either point the reference at a config with an emit directory, or (preferred) configure the reference's `outDir`/`tsBuildInfoFile` (e.g. `"./node_modules/.tmp"`) and add `"emitDeclarationOnly": true` in `tsconfig.node.json`.

No file under `src` imports with an explicit `.ts`/`.tsx` extension, so this flag currently buys nothing, but it permits imports like `./types.ts` that only work as long as `noEmit` stays `true` (tsc rejects them as soon as emit is enabled). It also ties the code to bundler-specific resolution. Recommend removing it to keep imports tool-agnostic.

`strict` leaves out the checks that matter most for this data-heavy codebase (heavy array/record indexing in `src/lib/grid.ts`, `src/lib/coords.ts`, `src/studio/*`). Consider enabling `"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true` and `"exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true` so out-of-range lookups and optional-vs-undefined property assignments are caught at compile time instead of yielding `undefined` at runtime.

`isolatedModules` is on, but `verbatimModuleSyntax` is not. Enabling it makes type-only imports/exports explicit at the syntax level, so a type that is imported or re-exported without `type` fails typechecking instead of relying on each transpiler's inference. The codebase already uses `import type` consistently, so this should cost nothing.

`skipLibCheck` speeds up builds but silences errors inside dependency typings. This project consumes large third-party type surfaces (`@univerjs/*`, `recharts`, `react-konva`), so a mismatch in their published `.d.ts` files is silently ignored and can turn into runtime failures. Keep it for day-to-day builds, but consider a CI-only pass without it (or pin the libs) so incompatible typings surface.

`default_objective` is `"tables"`, but the profile itself declares that the `voyage-supplement` genre is *not* a table (`"table_format": null`). A downstream consumer that seeds the project/study objective from this value would ask for tables on exactly the pages the profile says must not be annotated as tables. Either make the objective neutral (a sentence such as "extract ship registers") or move the objective inside `page_types` so each genre carries its own.

content: The page-type entries are symmetric in shape here (`description`, `recipe`, `table_format`), but `table_format` mixes types: `"otsl"` for one genre and `null` for the other. Consumers must special-case null instead of reading a single string contract. Since the recipe of `voyage-supplement` contains no `Table` label, a `null` is semantically "no table", which is better expressed by omitting the key (or by using an explicit sentinel such as `"none"` if the schema requires the key). As written, `null` is indistinguishable from "not configured yet".

The `conventions` and `labels` fields use bare-string shapes, but the per-project contracts are `list[ConventionItem]` (`id`, `label`, `checked`, with stable ids such as `soft_hyphen`, `sigle`, `colonne_fantasma`, `filetti`) and `LabelDef` (`name`, `color`, `short`, `prompt_kind`, `prompt`, `aliases`). A profile meant to seed a project cannot be fed to `PUT /api/projects/{id}/conventions` or merged into `projects.settings_json["labels"]` in this shape, and the rules here have no id to map onto the existing checklist. Use the same object shapes/ids (or add an explicit `id` per rule), or document these as names-only cross-references to `labeling.DEFAULT_LABELS`.

Nothing in the codebase reads `default_objective`, `page_types`, `conventions`, `labels`, `recommended_split` or `recommended_language`: `domain_profiles.list_profiles()` returns the raw dict and only `id` / `legacy_ids` are consumed (`canonical_id`, `get_profile`, `GET /api/system/domain-profiles`, and the UI which uses only `id` + `name`). A typo in any of these keys (or in `page_types` sub-keys such as `voyage-supplement`) would therefore stay invisible. Add a test/pydantic schema that asserts the exact key set of this file — e.g. `{"id", "legacy_ids", "name", "description", "labels", "page_types", "default_objective", "conventions", "recommended_split", "recommended_language"}` and, per page type, `{"description", "recipe", "table_format"}` — so key drift fails CI instead of silently disabling the profile.

The manifest declares neither the Node requirement (`engines` / `packageManager`) nor the Python prerequisite used by the `test:e2e:*` scripts, even though both are hard requirements: `vite@8` and `@vitejs/plugin-react@6` require `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0`, `@testing-library/jest-dom@7` requires `node >= 22`, and `../scripts/*.py` import `requests`, which is declared only in `backend/requirements.txt`. Contributors on older Node or a frontend-only setup get an opaque `EBADENGINE` / `ModuleNotFoundError` (or `python3: command not found`) instead of an actionable message. Declare the ranges and the Python requirement, or add a guard that fails fast with a clear message.

`tsc --noEmit` does not follow project references, so this script only checks `src` (tsconfig.json) and silently skips `tsconfig.node.json` (i.e. `vite.config.ts`). Use build mode so both projects are type-checked.

content: `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` does not make a failing native command terminate the script: on Windows PowerShell 5.1 it has no effect on `npm`, and on PowerShell 7.3+ it only applies when `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference` is enabled (off by default in 7.3). As a result a failed `npm ci` (lockfile mismatch, network/auth failure, Node too old, etc.) falls through and the script still prints ">> Frontend pronto.", falsely reporting success. The sibling `scripts/setup_backend.ps1` does check `$LASTEXITCODE`; do the same here. Note the bash counterpart uses `set -euo pipefail` and does fail correctly.

The target directory and the prerequisites of `npm ci` are never validated. `npm ci` requires both `frontend/` to exist and `frontend/package-lock.json` to be present (it refuses to run without a lockfile); when either is missing the failure surfaces as an opaque native-command error (and, given the missing exit-code check, potentially as a silent success). Add an explicit existence check with a clear diagnostic before invoking npm.

`npm run build` is a native command, so a non-zero exit code is not turned into a terminating error by `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` (and `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference` is not set, defaulting to false on PS 5.1 and PS 7). A failed build therefore falls through to the success message and the script exits 0 — and `scripts/run.ps1` (line 26) invokes this script with `&`, so it will keep booting the backend against a stale/missing `frontend/dist` while CI/automation sees success. Check `$LASTEXITCODE` explicitly right after `npm`.

`Set-Location` mutates the process-wide current directory and is never restored. When this script is dot-sourced or called in-session (as `scripts/run.ps1` does), the caller keeps running from `frontend`, so any relative path used afterwards resolves against the wrong directory. Use `Push-Location`/`Pop-Location` with a `try`/`finally` so the original location is restored even on failure.

`npm run dev` is a native command: `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` does NOT turn a non-zero exit status into a terminating error (and `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference` is not set). If Vite fails to start (missing node_modules, port in use, compile error on startup), the script still ends with exit code 0, so CI or a wrapper script that calls it will report success. Check `$LASTEXITCODE` and propagate it. Note the other sibling runner (`scripts/run_backend.ps1`) has the same gap, but the fix belongs to this file.
suggestion_code:
npm run dev
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit $LASTEXITCODE }

content: Catching the whole `sqlite3.Error` family silently turns real failures (corrupted file, `database is locked`, permission errors) into an empty config, so callers transparently fall back to env defaults instead of surfacing the problem. Restrict the tolerance to the case the docstring describes (a not-yet-initialised database) and let other errors propagate or at least log them.

`OperationalError` is not only raised for a missing pre-v10 `compute_profiles` table: it also covers `database is locked`, `readonly database` and malformed-schema errors. Swallowing all of them makes the transaction commit the `meta` upserts while leaving the active profile untouched, silently recreating the URL-from-one-provider/adapter-from-another bug this module documents against. def _redact(row: sqlite3.Row) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Hide credentials embedded in the recorded command line."""
    item = dict(row)
    try:
        command = json.loads(item.get("command_json") or "{}")
    except ValueError:
        return item
    argv = command.get("argv")
    if isinstance(argv, list):
        masked: list[str] = []
        hide_next = False
        for arg in argv:
            if hide_next:
                masked.append("***")
                hide_next = False
                continue
            if isinstance(arg, str) and arg in _SECRET_FLAGS:
                masked.append(arg)
                hide_next = True
                continue
            masked.append(arg)
        command["argv"] = masked
        item["command_json"] = json.dumps(command)
    return item

The function therefore rewrites the header as two levels and leaves the row-2 label cells untouched in the body (`cells if c["r"] >= 2`), producing a table whose first data row is nothing but header fragments — a silent corruption rather than a fail-closed return.

Add a check that the first preserved body row actually looks like data before rebuilding (or, symmetrically, that row 1 + row 2 do not both look like label rows).

For `k > n/2` the period test degenerates to a single comparison (`range(n - k)` has one element), so a spurious period is accepted on almost no evidence, and the code then unconditionally assumes the **last** group is the truncated one (`spans[-1] = n - (len(groups) - 1) * k`).

Concrete failure: 4 data columns, `row0 = ["NAME", "1908", "1909"]`, `leaves = ["Total", "Merch.", "Treas.", "Total"]` (the first year has a single aggregate column, the second has three). `k = 3` passes because `_same("Total", "Total")` is the only comparison, `len(groups) * k = 6 > 4`, so `spans = [3, 1]`: the two group titles are emitted over mirrored column ranges and the grid leaves the function looking repaired but wrong, with no fail-closed path.

Requiring at least two full repetitions (`n - k >= k`) keeps the intended truncated-tail case (`n=6, k=3`; `n=7, k=3`) while rejecting periods inferred from a single pair.

    k = (
        next(

                for k in range(2, n)
                if n - k >= k
                and all(_same(leaves[i], leaves[i + k]) for i in range(n - k))

            None,

        if len(leaves) == n
        else None

`value()` collapses two different states into `None`: "the surface does not exist" (`NotApplicable`) and "the surface exists but its declared value is `None`/falsy". `_ACTIVE` is mutated under `_LOCK` in `start_benchmark`, but the worker's cleanup runs without it and `benchmark_status` reads the dict without the lock. Two consequences: (1) a status poll landing between `_write_state(state="running")` and `_ACTIVE[project_id] = ...` sees `running` with no live thread and reports the run as interrupted; (2) between the `state="done"` write and this `pop`, a new `start_benchmark` sees the entry and wrongly reports `already_running`. Guard the pop (and ideally the read in `benchmark_status`) with `_LOCK`. Also note `_write_state` is a non-atomic read-modify-write: a concurrent reader can observe a half-written file and `benchmark_status` will then return `idle` while the benchmark is actually running — write to a temp file and `os.replace`.

Verify the process (e.g. match its command line against the recorded serve argv) before killing, or record a start time and compare it.

Additionally the corrected state (`serve_pid=None`) is only applied to the in-memory dict and never persisted, contrary to the comment: every subsequent status poll re-attempts the kill against the stale PID.

Unsynchronized check-then-act: the `is_ready()` check and `EnvBuilder(clear=True)` are not atomic, and `clear=True` wipes the whole `<root>/mlx-runtime` directory. Two callers that both see "not ready" (e.g. a start worker plus a retried `start()`, or a probe that fails transiently while the environment is actually fine) will delete the venv (`bin/python`, site-packages) out from under the concurrent `pip install` in the other thread, or destroy a usable, multi-GB environment and force a full re-download. Serialize provisioning with a module-level lock (and re-check `is_ready()` inside it) so a second caller waits/reuses instead of clearing.

content: `subprocess.run` here has no `timeout` and no `OSError`/`SubprocessError` handling. Two consequences: (1) if the interpreter exists but is not executable (broken symlink, no +x, quarantined binary) `subprocess.run` raises `PermissionError`/`OSError`, which propagates out of `is_ready()` and therefore out of `install_state()`, `ensure_ready()` and `serve_manager.start()` — the user sees a crash instead of "runtime not ready"; (2) importing `mlx_vlm.server` pulls in `mlx`/`transformers` and can take seconds or hang, blocking the caller (a start worker thread) indefinitely. The sibling `mineru_mlx_runtime.is_ready()` already wraps the probe in `try/except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError)` with `timeout=15`; do the same here and treat any failure as "not ready".

try:
        probe = subprocess.run(
            [str(python_bin()), "-c", "import mlx_vlm.server"],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=False,
            timeout=15,
        )
    except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError):
        return False
    return probe.returncode == 0

content: `json.loads` can return any JSON value, not just a dict: a corrupted/hand-edited or partially overwritten state file containing `null`, `[]` or a scalar makes `state.update(...)` raise `AttributeError` (not caught by `(OSError, ValueError)`), and the same happens with `stored.get(...)` in `install_state()`. Since this file is written non-atomically by `write_text`, a reader can also observe such content. Guard the type: fall back to `{}` when the parsed value is not a mapping.

When the persisted state says `ready` but `is_ready()` now returns False (venv partially removed, `mlx_vlm` broken by an upgrade, probe failure), this returns `{"ready": False, "state": "ready"}` — a client that trusts `state` reports a broken runtime as healthy, and `ensure_ready()` will only be reached if someone re-checks `ready` separately. Inconsistent pairs should not be produced: when the probe says not ready, the stored `ready` label must be downgraded (e.g. to `"stale"`/`"absent"`).

`connect` is imported but never used in this module (all DB access goes through `jobstore`). Drop the import; note that `time` is also re-imported locally in `_watch` even though it is already imported at module level.

The log file handle returned by `log_path.open("a")` is never closed by this process (the child inherits a duplicate, but the parent's descriptor stays open for the lifetime of the backend), so every setup/deploy/stop leaks one fd. Keep the handle in a `with` block around the `Popen` call, or store it on the task and close it once the watcher sees the process exit.

Only `sqlite3.OperationalError` is handled here. If `os.getpgid(proc.pid)` raises `OSError`/`ProcessLookupError`, or `jobstore.start_modal_job` raises anything else (e.g. `sqlite3.ProgrammingError`, `TypeError`), the exception propagates while the just-spawned `modal deploy` keeps running untracked and `_task` is never set — so `_persisted_running()` sees no row and a second deploy can be started on top of a live one. Wrap the bookkeeping in `except BaseException`/`except Exception`, terminate (and reap) the child, and only then re-raise.

`Popen` is launched without `start_new_session=True`, so the child stays in the backend's own process group and this stores the *backend's* pgid in the job row. Every later `os.killpg(process_group, ...)` on that value would signal Tabularium itself (including its server), and the `recovery_strategy='pid-process-group'` contract cannot be honoured. Start the subprocess in its own session/group and record the child's real group (`proc.pid` with `start_new_session=True`).

`process_group` is deliberately dropped from the recovered payload, so `_cancel_deploy_if_running()` always falls back to `persisted.get("process_group") or pid` and calls `os.killpg(pid, 15)`. Since the deploy process is not a group leader, that raises `ESRCH` (swallowed by the bare `except OSError: pass`), leaving the orphaned deploy alive right before `modal app stop`. Return the stored value here (once the child is spawned in its own session, see `_start`).

content: After terminating and waiting the deploy, `task.done` is only set later by the `_watch` thread (up to ~0.3 s, or never if the wait timed out). `stop_app()` calls `_start("stop", ...)` immediately after this function returns and `_start` rejects the launch while `_task is not None and not _task.done`, so a user-initiated stop can randomly fail with "un task Modal è già in corso". Mark the task finished here (under `_task_lock`) and reap the child in the timeout branch too (`kill()` without `wait()` may leave it running).

Concurrent writer on the same job row: the `_watch` thread also terminates this job via `jobstore.finish(job_id, "failed", returncode)` as soon as it observes the killed process, and `finish` has no `WHERE state='running'` guard. Depending on the thread interleaving the deliberate "deploy interrotto" record is overwritten by `failed`, so the recorded outcome of a cancelled deploy is non-deterministic. Either mark the task as cancelled so `_watch` skips the `finish` call, or make the update conditional on the current state.

A `TimeoutExpired` or malformed `--json` output is therefore reported to the UI as "not deployed" with no diagnostic anywhere in the logs. `drain()` re-reads and re-decodes the *entire* log file on every 0.3 s poll. content: `_RUNTIME_ACTIVE` is a module-level set shared by every request thread (both `/models` listing and start paths call `ensure_runtime_async`), and this check-then-act is not atomic: two concurrent callers can both pass the test before either calls `.add()`, spawning two threads that race on the same `.download_state.json` and on `paddle_runtime.ensure_ready()`. Guard the test-and-set with a `threading.Lock` (the same lock that protects `_ACTIVE` in `start_download`/`cancel_download`).

No mutual exclusion around the check/create/install sequence. `ensure_ready()` runs on a background `serve-start-*` thread (and the module has no lock, unlike `serve_manager._STARTING_LOCK`, which only guards a single process); a second caller — another thread retrying after a failed start, a direct `serve_manager.start()`, or the benchmark/CLI paths that share the same `ROOT_DIR` — can pass `is_ready() is False` while the first pip run is still writing. Because the rebuild uses `clear=True`, it then deletes the venv out from under the running install, so both fail with a corrupted runtime. Guard the whole sequence with a process-wide lock (and ideally a lock file for cross-process use).

Destructive rebuild on a transient probe failure: `is_ready()` uses a 15 s `subprocess.run(..., timeout=15)`, and `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` (caught as `SubprocessError`) is reported as "not ready". On a slow/loaded machine the probe can time out while the venv is perfectly fine, and `ensure_ready()` then answers with `venv.EnvBuilder(clear=True)`, which deletes the existing runtime directory (and its `.install.log`/`.install_state.json`) and forces a full multi-hundred-MB reinstall. Distinguish "probe failed/timed out" from "venv absent", e.g. retry the probe once or only clear after confirming the interpreter really is broken/half-installed.

The `pip install` calls run without a `timeout` and the state file was set to `"installing"` just above. A stalled network / hung resolver leaves the thread blocked indefinitely (it is the background `serve-start` worker) and the state permanently stuck in `installing`; the UI then shows a preparation that never progresses. Pass an explicit `timeout` (and reset the state to `error` on `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`, which is not covered by the current `except`).

Two robustness problems in the state persistence: (1) `json.loads` may legitimately return a non-dict (e.g. `[]` or a bare string left by a truncated/interrupted write) and `state.update(...)` then raises `AttributeError`, which is not covered by the `(OSError, ValueError)` guard and would abort `ensure_ready()` after the venv was already rebuilt; `install_state()` has the same `stored.get(...)` assumption. (2) `write_text` is not atomic: an interruption mid-write truncates the file, silently losing the state (which the code then papers over as `{}`). Validate the parsed value and write via a temp file + `os.replace()`.

When the stored state is `"ready"` but `is_ready()` now returns False (venv deleted, Python upgraded, dependency pruned, probe timeout), this returns the contradictory payload `{"ready": False, "state": "ready"}`. Any caller that branches on `state` instead of `ready` will show the runtime as ready and skip the reinstall path. Downgrade a stale `ready` label to something neutral.

The readiness probe only checks that the distributions are *present* (`importlib.util.find_spec` does not import top-level modules) plus metadata versions. A venv whose native MLX extension is broken (wrong wheel/arch, missing shared lib, half-finished install) is therefore reported as ready, and the failure only surfaces later inside the gateway process with an opaque message. The sibling `mlx_runtime.is_ready()` actually imports the module — do the same here. Note also that the probe hard-codes `mlx-vlm` 0.7.x while `PACKAGES` does not pin it: if the resolution picks another minor, the install "succeeds" and then fails right here with `installazione ... incompleta`, which is misleading. Pin it explicitly or drop the gate.

`valid` is built from `canonical.values()`, i.e. from the *normalized* dict, not from the real class names. Two project labels whose names differ only by separators (`"Vessel Name"` and `"Vessel_Name"`) are both accepted by `labeling.project_schema`/`validate_labels` (they are compared with `==`, not normalized), but here they collapse to a single key: the dict keeps only the last name, so the other real class is missing from `valid` and every adapter mapping that targets it is silently rejected (falls through to `None`). content: The exact-canonical branch runs before the adapter map for *every* adapter, including the ones that declare a native map. That is fine when the vendor token really is the canon, but a project class whose normalized name coincides with a vendor token hijacks the mapping: with a custom class `Header` (allowed by `_NAME_RE`), MinerU/GLM/Paddle `header` resolves to that custom class instead of `Page-header` from the adapter map, contradicting the docstring's rule that the model's semantics win. Consider consulting the adapter map first when the adapter has one (models that speak the canon, e.g. MonkeyOCRv2, have no map, so they still hit this branch).

`known_models_for` recomputes the whole adapter registry per name, and `list_adapters()` also queries `custom_models.list_all()` (a DB read) and builds a `CustomVllmAdapter` per custom row. The only caller (`api/blocks.py::_label_schema`) invokes this once per label of the schema (~15+), so a single request triggers N registry rebuilds and N DB round-trips for an O(adapters) answer. Expose a single inverse index (class -> adapters) computed once, or accept the already-listed capabilities.

`NATIVE_LABELS` is derived from immutable specs, so its keys never change, yet every call re-normalizes all of them (up to ~28 entries for MinerU) with a regex. This is called once per parsed block in `prefill.py` and per prediction in `evaluate.py`, so the work is repeated thousands of times per page. Precompute a normalized map at import time (e.g. `_NORMALIZED_NATIVE = {adapter_id: {normalize_label(k): v ...}}`) and iterate over that.

_MLX_LIMITS is shared by several integer knobs, but `kv_bits` is the only one cast to `float`. `save_settings` persists the override, and `serve_manager`/`mlx_runtime.serve_argv` forward it to `mlx-vlm` as `str(value)` → the flag becomes `--kv-bits 4.0`, while `kv_group_size`, `max_kv_size` and `vision_cache_size` stay integers. Worse, the range check `2 <= value <= 8` lets fractional inputs (e.g. `4.5`) through unchanged, so a half bit width reaches the KV-cache quantizer. Cast `kv_bits` to `int` like its siblings (and reject fractional values, see the truncation comment below).

content: Integer-valued knobs are silently truncated instead of rejected: `max_model_len=1024.5`, `max_num_seqs=2.7`, `max_tokens=100.9`, `max_pixels=1e6+0.5`, `kv_group_size=32.5` all pass the range check and are then coerced with `int(value)`. The workflow validator already rejects fractional ints (`kind == "int" and int(value) != value`), so this inconsistency lets the panel/API store a value the user never entered and the served CLI will differ from what was validated. The same `int(...)` coercion exists in the serving branch (line 237), the MLX guard branch (line 270) and the MLX limits branch (line 275); validate `int(value) != value` for the integer keys, e.g. with a small helper.

`repo_choices` and the `mlx_enums` values are `set`s, and the membership test is done without a type guard: a JSON payload such as `{"mlx": {"repo": ["a"]}}` or `{"mlx": {"kv_quant_scheme": {"a": 1}}}` makes `value not in <set>` raise `TypeError: unhashable type`, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 instead of the intended 422 (the serving branch avoids this by checking `isinstance(value, str)` first). Add the same string guard here, and to `value not in mlx_enums[key]` on line 262.

`_validate_workflow` validates the cross-field `requires` rules against `stored overrides + result`, but `save_settings` persists only `result`: the stored workflow overrides used here are dropped by this very write. The check therefore evaluates a state that never exists, in both directions. It can reject a valid save — with `cost_optimizer: true` stored while `tier` is the default `agentic`, sending `{"workflow": {"tier": "cost_effective"}}` fails with "cost_optimizer richiede tier" even though the save would leave `cost_optimizer` at its default. And it can accept a combination whose meaning changes after the write: `tier: agentic_plus` stored plus `{"cost_optimizer": true}` passes only because the stored `tier` is merged in, and that override is then discarded. Merge only `spec.workflow_defaults()` with `result` (the state that will actually exist), or persist the merged view consistently.

`TABULARIUM_OPENCODE_AUTH` is documented as an override, but the default archive is still appended and searched afterwards. If the custom archive is missing, empty or malformed (e.g. an isolated test fixture that has no `opencode-go` entry), the function silently falls back to the real user credentials in `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`. That breaks test isolation and hides configuration errors. When the env var is set it should be the only candidate considered.

Any read/parse failure is discarded silently, so a typo in `TABULARIUM_OPENCODE_AUTH`, an unreadable file or a corrupt auth.json is indistinguishable from "no key configured". The caller only sees an empty string and the resulting authentication error is opaque. At minimum log a warning (without leaking key material) so misconfiguration can be diagnosed; the distinction between "file absent" and "file present but unparsable" is the actionable one.

Coercing the stored value with `str(...)` means any truthy non-string value (a nested dict, a list, a number) is returned as a "key" and reported as available by `status()`, although it can never be a valid token. Validate the type instead of stringifying arbitrary data, so a malformed archive is treated as "no key" rather than as a usable credential.

`_ensure` deliberately supports PaddleOCR 2.x (it accepts `use_angle_cls`/`show_log`), but `detect` only uses the 3.x API: PaddleOCR 2.x has no `predict()` method (only `ocr()`/`__call__`), and its result is a list of `[box, (text, score)]`, not dict-like pages. With a 2.x install the engine initializes fine and then blows up with `AttributeError` on the first page. Either detect drops 2.x support (and `_ensure` should not pretend to support it) or the parsing must branch on the PaddleOCR major version.

A config-forced engine is returned without any check that the package is importable, so `OcrEngine.available` (and the `/api/system` health payload built from `available_engine()`) reports `True` when e.g. `TABULARIUM_OCR_ENGINE=paddleocr` but paddleocr is not installed; `_ensure()` then raises `ImportError` mid-run in code that already guarded on `.available` (e.g. `prefill.py` layout fallback). Verify the module exists (and warn about the ignored forcing) instead of returning it unconditionally.

Every new login wipes **all** in-flight state rows, not just the caller's. Two users starting a login at the same time (or one user with two tabs) delete each other's row and the second callback fails with `oidc_state`; the delete is also racy against a concurrent `put`, which can be removed right after being written. The single-use guarantee already comes from `store.pop()` in `consume_state`, so the blanket prefix delete is not needed for correctness. If the goal is to bound table growth, purge only rows whose `expires_at` is already in the past (e.g. `store.delete_expired_prefix(...)`) instead of dropping live states.

The scheme check accepts plaintext `http://` for the authorization endpoint and, more importantly, never validates `token_endpoint` (used in `exchange_code`) or `userinfo_endpoint`. A discovery document served over TLS can therefore point at `http://…` endpoints and the client secret, authorization code and access token/token response all travel in clear text — contradicting the module docstring's "read from `/userinfo` over TLS" premise. Require `https://` for all three endpoints (allowing `http://` only for an explicit localhost dev override) and check the token/userinfo URLs here, before they are cached.

`response.json()` can legally return a list, string or number; the subsequent `document.get(...)` then raises `AttributeError`, which is neither an `httpx.HTTPError` nor a `ValueError`, so it escapes the `OidcError` contract and becomes an unhandled 500 in `oidc_callback`/`oidc_start`. Validate `isinstance(document, dict)` and raise `OidcError("oidc_discovery", ...)` on anything else.

Same problem as the discovery document: an error/HTML-ish JSON payload that decodes to a list or scalar makes `tokens.get("access_token")` raise `AttributeError` outside the `except (httpx.HTTPError, ValueError)` clause, producing a 500 instead of an `oidc_exchange` error. Guard with `if not isinstance(tokens, dict): raise OidcError("oidc_exchange", ...)`.

Only a literal `False` is rejected, so an email whose verification is unknown slips through: providers that omit `email_verified` entirely (allowed by the spec for `/userinfo`) and providers that send it as the string `"false"` both pass, and the address is then accepted by the domain allowlist and used to create/link an account. Normalise the claim so string values cannot be interpreted as verified, and make the missing-claim policy explicit rather than implicit (reject, or document/report why it is trusted).

`_last_error` is a single module-level slot written by every call. `dewarp.align_page` (used by `POST /api/pages/{id}/align`) calls `preprocess()` **without** the `_transform_lock` that `run_transform` holds, and FastAPI runs sync endpoints in a thread pool, so two concurrent pages can overwrite each other's error. The caller then reads `last_error()` and may report another page's failure (or `None`, falling back to the generic `monkeyocr_preprocessor_unavailable`). Each concurrent call also spawns its own Python process that reloads both nets, which is expensive on CPU-only. Return the error together with the result (e.g. a small result object/tuple) or keep it per-thread (`threading.local()`), and consider serialising the subprocess call like `run_transform` does.

`available()`, `python_bin()` and `tempfile.mkdtemp()` run outside the `try`, so an OSError from `mkdtemp` (full/permission-denied tmpdir, mis-configured `config.SERVE_PYTHON` path) or from the file-system checks inside `available()` propagates to the caller instead of returning `None` as the docstring promises. The callers (`dewarp.align_page` / `_run_transform_locked`) do not wrap this call in a try block, so the request fails with a 500 instead of falling back to deskew.

tmp: Path | None = None
    try:
        interpreter = python_bin()
        tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="monkeypre_"))
        # ... existing body ...
    finally:
        if tmp is not None:
            import shutil

            shutil.rmtree(tmp, ignore_errors=True)

content: The module docstring says the official runner uses `preprocess_images()`, but the subprocess calls the singular `preprocess_image`. If the vendored `Preprocessor` only exposes the plural method, every attempt dies with `AttributeError`, the code silently falls back to deskew and the neural path is effectively dead (only visible as a stderr tail in the diagnostics). Please confirm the vendored API and align the docstring with the actual call.

The wheel is chosen purely from the driver's CUDA version, which contradicts the rationale in the docstring: a Blackwell host whose driver advertises 12.8 (a very common state) falls into the `>= 12.6` branch and gets `cu126`, while the docstring states that Blackwell (SM 12.0) needs `cu129` and that a previous cu118 default was invalid for the RTX PRO 4000. Either the Blackwell detection should be explicit (e.g. `torch.cuda.get_device_capability`/`nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap`) or the 12.8 driver case should be routed to `cu129` so the code matches the documented requirement.

When the override is set, the `paddleocr[doc-parser]` installation is skipped entirely, so unless the operator also lists it in `TABULARIUM_PADDLE_PACKAGES` the final `from paddleocr import PaddleOCRVL` check fails and the whole install is marked `failed` with an error that does not point at the override. `override.split()` also breaks any specifier/URL containing spaces. Consider keeping the doc-parser install unconditional (letting the override only replace the Paddle wheel) or validating the override and reporting a clear error.

`Path.write_text` truncates the file before writing, so the read-modify-write is not atomic: a `status()` call racing with the installer can read an empty/partial file, fall into the `except ValueError` branch of `status()` and report `state="absent"` — exactly the symptom the comment in `ensure_ready` says must not happen during installation. Two concurrent writers can also lose fields. Write to a temp file in the same directory and `os.replace()` it for an atomic swap.

`state="installing"` is persisted before `log_path().open("ab")`, and the `open()` itself sits outside the guarded `try/except`. If the log cannot be opened (permissions, full disk, file locked on Windows) the exception escapes as a raw `OSError` and the persisted state stays `installing` forever, so `status(probe=False)` keeps reporting an install in progress. The final `_write_state(state="ready")` below has the same problem in the opposite direction: if it fails, a working runtime is reported as still installing. Move the `open()` under the `try` (and record `failed`) and consider wrapping the final ready write as well.

`ensure_ready()` is invoked from a background thread per adapter (`model_registry.ensure_runtime_async` starts one thread per adapter_id and `_RUNTIME_ACTIVE` is keyed by adapter, not by runtime). Since several adapters share the paddle runtime (`paddleocr-vl`, `xiaomi-ocr-0`), two threads can pass the `ready()` check simultaneously and both run `venv.EnvBuilder(clear=True).create(root)` plus `pip install` on the same directory: the second `clear=True` wipes the venv while the first is installing into it, and the interleaved pip runs can leave a broken environment that still gets marked `ready`. Guard the whole installation with a module-level `threading.Lock` (re-checking `ready()` inside the lock) so only one install can run at a time.

Duplicate plugin ids are silently overwritten: registering an adapter with an id that already exists (e.g. a typo such as "builtin-scan ") makes the previously registered/built-in descriptor unreachable with no error or warning. Since `register_plugin` is the public entry point and is called by adapter modules at import time, a silent shadowing is hard to diagnose. Reject duplicates (or require an explicit `overwrite=True` flag) and raise/return an error so the collision is visible.

existing = _REGISTRY.get(descriptor.plugin_id)
    if existing is not None:
        raise ValueError(f"plugin_id già registrato: {descriptor.plugin_id}")
    _REGISTRY[descriptor.plugin_id] = descriptor
    return descriptor

Normalize the id and restrict `kind` to the known set of plugin kinds so malformed descriptors cannot enter the registry.

content: Reading `descriptor.__dict__` bypasses the dataclass API: it silently breaks if the dataclass ever declares `slots=True`, and it couples the public API output to internal attribute layout. Use `dataclasses.asdict()` (already importing from `dataclasses`) so the serialization stays consistent with the declared fields.

content: Gold-page protection is all-or-nothing and silently disabled: the whole `protected` set is built in one comprehension inside a `try` that swallows `TypeError`/`ValueError` without logging. A single non-numeric entry in `gold_pages` (e.g. a typo in `settings_json`) yields an empty set, so the study-protocol gold pages end up in the pilot sample without any warning. In addition, if `study_protocol` is present but not a dict (`None`, list, string), `.get` raises `AttributeError`, which is not in the caught tuple and will propagate out of the sampler.
`json` is imported but never used in this module — dead import (likely a leftover from an earlier implementation).

When the stored boundary count does not match `count + 1` the function silently substitutes perfectly uniform spacing. For any table whose real column/row boundaries are uneven (merged headers, varying column widths), every cell crop is then cut on the wrong offsets and the rec targets are silently corrupted, with nothing in `warnings`/manifest telling the caller the geometry was approximated. The caller should at least be able to distinguish "real boundaries" from "fallback" (return a flag, or skip the table and append a warning) instead of the fallback being invisible.

lines = [float(v) for v in (grid.get(axis) or [])]
    if len(lines) == count + 1:

The same applies to `float(v)` inside `_grid_lines`, which raises on a `None` entry in `vlines`/`hlines`.

content: `build` already holds the full `collect_pages_with_blocks(project_id)` result in `data`, but `compute_split` collects it all over again (DB queries plus JSON parsing of every table grid). On big projects the export therefore loads the whole project twice. Consider passing the already-collected mapping (or a page-id/status pre-filter) so the second full pass is avoided.

`unverified_skipped` is only incremented in the `approved_only` branch, so the manifest warning based on it can never fire in the `approved_only=False` build — precisely the mode where prefill text that nobody verified is written into `rec_train.txt` and silently becomes gold training data. Track the included unverified cells too (e.g. `rec_cells["unverified_included"]`) and warn on that in the non-approved build, so the caller is told that unverified labels entered the rec dataset.

The COCO `file_name` is not relative to the dataset directory: `builder._page_image_path` returns the original absolute source path for `source_kind == "image"` (and an absolute path under `crops/` for rendered PDFs). The copy written to `annotations/train.json|val.json` therefore keeps those absolute paths, so the exported layout dataset is not self-contained — moving it (or the project data dir) to a training host breaks every image reference, and image-kind pages point outside `out` entirely. Either copy/link the page images under `out` and store paths relative to `out` (e.g. `crops/page_42.png`), or at minimum record in the manifest that the paths are absolute.

All the manifest warnings are hard-coded Italian strings, while the rest of the dataset pipeline goes through `services.i18n.msg(...)` (see `dataset_builder._write_crop`/`_page_image_path`) and the API routes resolve the request language. Callers on an `en`/`fr` UI get Italian diagnostics, and the strings are duplicated rather than added to the shared catalogue. Accept a `lang` parameter (the endpoint already has access to `Accept-Language`) and route these messages through `msg`.

`subprocess.run` is given a timeout, but `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` (and `FileNotFoundError`/`OSError` from a stale `paddle_runtime.python_bin()`) is never caught here. Everything else in this function is converted into a friendly `RuntimeError`, so a hung pipeline instead surfaces a raw `TimeoutExpired` with the whole `cmd` in its message; callers such as `api/playground.py` then wrap it in a misleading `503 "vLLM non raggiungibile"`. Wrap the call and re-raise as `RuntimeError` (with `from exc`).

Same gap as `parse_page`: `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` (and `OSError` when the runtime interpreter has disappeared since `paddle_runtime.ready()`) escapes unwrapped. Since this runs on the Xiaomi-OCR region path, the raw exception also skips the `RuntimeError` contract the rest of the function honours.

Two robustness gaps here:
1. `.get("path", "")` assumes the last stdout line loads to a `dict`. If a dependency flushes a bare JSON scalar/array as the last line, this raises `AttributeError`, which is not in the `except` tuple, so it escapes as a raw exception instead of the intended `RuntimeError`.
2. Only the *last* line is parsed as JSON, but the runner's `print` is followed by interpreter shutdown, where PaddleX/Paddle logs can still be flushed to stdout; a trailing log line silently turns a successful run into "output JSON PaddleOCRVL non valido".
Scanning stdout in reverse for the first line that decodes to a dict fixes both.

`hinted` is read straight out of the subprocess stdout (or could be relative to the server's CWD) and is used without checking that it stays inside `root`, the temp dir this call owns. A bug in the runner/`save_to_json`, or a hint that is a relative or unrelated absolute path, makes `parse_page` read an arbitrary file as the page result. Restrict the hint to the output directory and fall back to the scan otherwise.

The documented fallback ("keep the recursive fallback for older PaddleX schemas") only runs when `parsing_res_list` is *missing*, not when it is present but empty. With `parsing_res_list: []` and detections only in `layout_det_res`, `_items([])` returns `[]`, the guard is skipped, and the layout projection is never consulted, so those regions are silently dropped (only the markdown fallback can save the page). If an empty canonical list should not suppress the fallback, walk `root` in that case too.

`conn` is not defined anywhere in this module (only `connect` is imported), so the first time a missing thumbnail is generated the JPEG is written to disk and then `pagestore.set_thumb(conn, ...)` raises `NameError` → HTTP 500. Every subsequent call also returns the file but the DB `thumb_path` is never updated. `ensure_thumbnail` is called from the API route without any connection in scope, so the service must open its own connection (and commit it).

        pagestore.set_thumb(conn, page["id"], str(expected))

content: Bulk approval does not enforce the gold-page rule that single-page `approve_page` enforces: pages protected by the study protocol are set to `approved` here even without a passing review, bypassing `_gold_pages` + `has_passing_review`. A gold page must not be approvable through the bulk path.

Two fragile assumptions here: (1) `settings.get('study_protocol', {})` can legitimately be `None`, a list or a string (settings JSON is user-editable and `settings_json` only guarantees the top-level object), so `.get(...)` may raise `AttributeError`; (2) a single malformed entry in `gold_pages` makes `int(value)` raise `ValueError`, which the comprehension aborts into the `except` and returns an *empty* set — silently disabling protection for all valid gold pages. Parse defensively and keep the valid entries.

The `try` only guards `json.loads`, but a stored value of `'null'` (or another valid non-list JSON such as `'3'`) parses without error into `None`/int, and the following `len(points)` raises an uncaught `TypeError`, turning a readiness check into a 500 instead of a readiness error. Guard the type too.

The cached tile is returned before any invalidation check, and the cache key (page id + level + x/y, plus `_level.jpg`) does not include `TRANSFORM_VERSION` or the transform identity. If the master is swapped or a transform becomes invalid without going through the API's `_invalidate_page_cache`, stale tiles rendered from the old/invalid canvas keep being served indefinitely. Run `_purge_invalid_transform(page)` before short-circuiting on the cached file (as `ensure_thumbnail`/`ensure_preview` do).

    _purge_invalid_transform(page)
    if out.exists():
        return out

content: `grid_json` is decoded without any guard, while `_compute_readiness` explicitly wraps the same value in `try/except (TypeError, ValueError)`. A corrupted/legacy `grid_json` therefore makes the confirm/approval flow raise `json.JSONDecodeError` (500) instead of reporting an invalid grid. Skip rows whose JSON cannot be parsed (or re-raise as a domain error).

`Path(...).stem` strips only the last suffix, so a name such as `LSI_17186_015.tar.gz` (or `LSI_17186_015.tif.bak`) yields the stem `LSI_17186_015.tar`, which the anchored `_PATTERN` rejects. The function then silently returns an empty `FileMeta()`, so `issue_no`/`page_no`/`page_type` are dropped without any signal, contradicting the docstring's "con estensione qualsiasi" claim. Stripping every suffix (first dot of the basename) fixes this, since the pattern only allows letters/digits/underscores in the meaningful part.

content:
Read-then-act across separate non-atomic store calls. `window()` runs a SELECT and `bump()`/`start()` run their own UPDATE/UPSERT, each on a fresh connection (endpoints are sync `def`, so FastAPI dispatches them to a thread pool and several workers may run at once). Two consequences:
1. N concurrent login attempts all read `attempts < limit` and all increment, so the effective cap is unbounded — the brute-force protection this module exists for is bypassed by parallelizing requests.
2. Worse, when the window is missing/expired each concurrent request calls `start()`, and the adapter's `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET ..., attempts=1` rewrites the row: a burst of parallel attempts keeps resetting the counter to 1, so the limit is never reached at all.
The check and the increment must happen in a single atomic statement (e.g. one UPSERT that increments only `WHERE window_started > :now - :window AND attempts < :limit` and reports the affected row count), and the service should derive the boolean from that result instead of from the value read beforehand.
existing_code:
now = time.time()
    current = store.window(key)
    if current is None or now - current[0] >= window:
        store.start(key, now)
        return True

content: The result of `store.bump()` is discarded, and the adapter's bump is `UPDATE ... WHERE key=?`, which silently affects 0 rows when the row was deleted between the read and the write (e.g. a concurrent successful login calls `reset()`, or the window row was replaced/removed by another caller). In that case `allow()` returns True without recording the attempt, letting the attempt go uncounted indefinitely. Either have the adapter return `cursor.rowcount` and treat 0 as "window gone, start a new one", or fold the increment into the same atomic statement as the check.
existing_code:
if current[1] >= limit:
        return False
    store.bump(key)
    return True

content: The window is measured with the wall clock, which is not monotonic: an NTP/manual backward step makes `now - current[0]` negative, so the condition is false and an already expired window is kept alive (legitimate users stay locked out longer), while a forward step discards an in-progress window (limit bypass). `time.monotonic()` cannot be used as-is because the timestamp is persisted and shared across processes/restarts, so at minimum clamp the elapsed value: compute `elapsed = now - current[0]` and treat `elapsed < 0` as expired (start a new window).
suggestion_code: now = time.time()

content: The project (and therefore `owner_id`) is read on its own connection *before* the write transaction is opened. Concurrent requests run in the FastAPI threadpool, so between `projectstore.get()` and `writer.put_member()` a `transfer_owner` call can make `user_id` the owner; the invariant "owner cannot also be a member" is then violated in the database (no constraint/trigger enforces it), leaving the project with a member row for its own owner. Re-read `owner_id` inside the same transaction (e.g. a `writer.owner_id(project_id)` helper) and validate there.

`transfer_owner` also branches on the `owner_id` snapshot taken before the transaction. A concurrent transfer can make `old_owner` stale, so this code overwrites the newer owner with `set_owner()` and demotes the wrong user to `editor`, and the audit `from_user_id` lies. Read the current owner inside the writing transaction before deciding what to write.

The previous owner is re-added as `editor` without checking `target`-style active status, which contradicts the rule stated in this module's docstring ("only an active account can be added"). A deactivated account therefore regains read/write membership on the project after a transfer. Check the former owner's `active` flag and only add the membership when it is true.

                writer.put_member(project_id, old_owner, "editor")

Validate against the allowed roles (`authsvc.PROJECT_ROLES - {"owner"}`) and raise a 400 before writing.

A process whose command line contains bytes that are not valid in that encoding (quite possible: argv is arbitrary bytes on POSIX) makes `subprocess.run` raise `UnicodeDecodeError`, which is a `ValueError` and therefore not covered by the `(OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError)` handler below. The exception then escapes `_ps_field` and breaks `process_state`/`is_zombie`/`process_cmdline` callers (e.g. `_pid_alive` polling loops) instead of degrading to `None` as the contract says. Decode explicitly with replacement characters.

            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            encoding="utf-8",
            errors="replace",
            timeout=_PS_TIMEOUT,
        )

content: The two platform branches do not return the same shape for the same situation: here the trailing NUL becomes a trailing space and an empty `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` (kernel threads, zombies) yields `""`, while the macOS branch strips the output and maps empty to `None`. Returning `""` instead of `None` also contradicts the docstring contract ("None when not readable") and silently turns an unreadable command line into a "readable but empty" one for callers that distinguish the two. Normalize both sides: strip the trailing separator and return `None` when the result is empty.

                Path(f"/proc/{pid}/cmdline")
                .read_bytes()
                .replace(b"\0", b" ")
                .decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                .rstrip()
            )
            return command or None

Only the local ssh client is signalled; the remote pip/venv process keeps running and can hold `/opt/tabularium/eval-venv`, so a retry races with the orphaned installer. Wait for the process and kill it if it does not exit.

The socket is closed before the SSH tunnel binds the port, so another process can take it in between; `_wait_port` then fails with "SSH tunnel is unavailable" for a reason unrelated to the tunnel. Prefer letting ssh bind port 0 / retry the port allocation when `_wait_port` fails, or pick a remote-free local port and retry a few times on failure.

This rule exempts *every* surface of a runtime-registered model, including `capabilities` and `settings`, which do exist for them (`model_settings.get_settings("custom-…")` resolves through `get_adapter`, and `_presence("capabilities")` returns True by construction). Two consequences:
1. The matrix reports `not_applicable` for surfaces that are in fact declared, which is exactly the "false story" the module claims to prevent.
2. It contradicts `test_every_model_has_serving_settings` in `backend/tests/test_model_surface.py`, which asserts `row.state("settings").state == "declared"` for every row of `matrix()` — so the suite fails on any machine that has a custom model registered in its DB.
Better: only exempt the surfaces a custom checkpoint genuinely cannot declare (`serve`, `labels`, `train`) and let `capabilities`/`settings` be validated normally.

        return False, "checkpoint registered at runtime: its surfaces are the registry row"

The `except` comment says "Unknown adapter", but an unknown adapter makes `get_adapter` raise `ValueError`, never `KeyError`. content: The vault is mutated (`put`/`delete`) before the issuer, client_id, scopes and allowed-domain validations run. Any later `ValueError` aborts the save with the settings JSON untouched but the secret already overwritten or deleted — leaving partial, inconsistent state (e.g. the old secret is gone while the UI still shows the old configuration). Perform all validation first, then mutate the vault, ideally together with the `store.put`.

`verify_password` assumes the stored material is well-formed: `bytes.fromhex(salt_hex)` raises `ValueError` on non-hex/odd-length input and `TypeError` when the column is `NULL`, and `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` if `hash_hex` is not ASCII. `services/auth.check_password` (auth.py:75) passes DB values straight through and the login endpoint does not catch anything, so a corrupted/legacy row turns into a 500 instead of a controlled 401. Parse defensively and compare raw digests instead of hex strings.

The docstring promises a new salt only when `salt is None`, but the truthiness test also discards an empty string (and `bytes.fromhex("")` would yield a zero-length salt anyway, which is never a valid stored value). A caller passing `""` by mistake silently gets a different salt than the one it thinks it is reusing, hiding real bugs. Use an explicit `is not None` check and validate the decoded length/format.

content: The KDF parameters are not stored alongside the digest: `hash_password` writes `salt`/`password_hash` only, so raising `PBKDF2_ITERATIONS` later makes every existing hash unverifiable (all logins fail with 401) with no way to distinguish old from new rows — there is no upgrade path without a migration. Also note 210k iterations for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 is below the OWASP baseline (600k) as of this writing. Encode the algorithm and iteration count in the stored value (e.g. `pbkdf2_sha256$210000$<salt>$<hash>`) and parse it in `verify_password`, falling back to the legacy bare-hex format with an opportunistic rehash on successful login.

`password.encode("utf-8")` raises `UnicodeEncodeError` for lone-surrogate strings, which a JSON payload such as `"\ud800"` can produce. Login calls this on attacker-controlled input, so a malformed password yields a 500 instead of a 401 (the same issue exists in `hash_password`). Encode with `errors="surrogatepass"` in both functions (so hashing and verification stay consistent) or reject such input during validation.

    digest = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac(

content: `ready()` runs `compute_readiness`, which loads every block of the page and parses each table grid, while the `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` RESERVED lock acquired at the top of `submit` is still held. SQLite allows a single writer, so every concurrent submission/assignment queues on this lock for the whole scan (up to the 30 s `busy_timeout` configured in `db.connect`). Compute readiness *before* acquiring the write lock, then re-validate `version`/`annotation_revision` after `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` so the TOCTOU window stays closed.

`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` is taken before this authorization check, so a caller who is not a manager (e.g. any project editor spamming PUT /work) still grabs the RESERVED write lock on every rejected request and serializes all other writers. All validations that only need reads (`workstore.page`, `get_work`, this permission check) can run before `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`; take the lock only right before `upsert`.

The run also stays `queued` in SQLite with no worker. The leaked id then makes `reconcile_runs()` skip this run forever (it is treated as "still alive" after a restart of the lifespan) and `cancel_run()` sets an event nobody reads. Wrap the start in try/except and roll back both the dict entry and the run state.

content: The resource identity used to stop the cloud instance is read from the *live* inference config at release time, not from what the run actually used (the run row has no `resource_id`). If the user reconfigures the endpoint (new Vast instance, switch to RunPod) while a long session is running, this code stops the instance currently in the config — i.e. possibly a different, maybe more recently rented GPU — while the one that did the work keeps running. The docstring explicitly promises "l'istanza esatta registrata dalla run", but nothing binds it to the run. Record `resource_id`/`provider_credential_ref` on the run at creation and release from those values (and only fall back to the config when they are absent).

`active_ids` is snapshotted under the lock and then the lock is released before `runstore.reconcile()` queries the DB. Between the two statements another request/thread can insert a `queued` run and register it in `_ACTIVE`; the snapshot will not contain it and `reconcile()` will mark that live run and its items as `failed`. Since the module comment acknowledges re-entrant lifespans, take the snapshot and perform the reconcile under the same lock (or exclude runs whose `job_id` was created after startup) so the read-modify-write stays consistent with `_start_worker`.

The `"ocr"` fallback in `getattr` can never trigger: `OcrEngine.name` always exists, it is just the empty string when no OCR backend is installed (`available_engine()` returns `None`). So an OCR run started on a machine without RapidOCR/PaddleOCR is recorded with `model_name=''` instead of the intended `'ocr'`. Use an explicit fallback, e.g. `ocrmod.OcrEngine().name or "ocr"`, which also avoids the dead `getattr` default.

`_terminate()` returns `False` when the process survives both SIGTERM and SIGKILL, but the result is discarded: the job is marked `stopped` and `_ACTIVE_PROC`/`_ACTIVE_INFO` are cleared anyway. A still-live vLLM keeps the GPU and the port, yet this module forgets it — and the next `start()` will find the port busy with a PID it can no longer attribute. Only clear the bookkeeping (and mark the job stopped) when the process is really gone; otherwise keep the handle and surface the failure.

`start()` is normally invoked from the daemon thread created in `start_async()`, and Python documents `preexec_fn` as unsafe in a multi-threaded process: after the fork the child can deadlock on an inherited lock before `exec`. `start_new_session=True` gives the same `setsid()` semantics without running Python in the child.

Since the sole current caller passes a Pydantic-validated `str` the blast radius is limited, but the signature advertises `object`, so a future programmatic caller can persist a misleading hint.             size = fh.tell()

            data = fh.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")

content: Only `CalledProcessError` and `TimeoutExpired` are translated into the intended contextual `RuntimeError`. If `git` is not installed, `subprocess.run` raises `FileNotFoundError`, and permission/disk errors raise `OSError` from both `subprocess.run` and the `shutil.rmtree`/`mkdir` above; all of them escape with an unrelated low-level message (e.g. `[Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'git'`). Add an `OSError` branch (FileNotFoundError is a subclass) that reports git missing / clone not possible.

The check-then-act on `target` is not atomic and the clone writes directly into the final path: if two `start()` calls run at the same time (the only current caller, `serve_manager.start_async`, is single-flight, but `start()` is public and also invoked directly, e.g. from tests/CLI), one call can `rmtree` the directory the other is cloning into, leaving both with a corrupted checkout. Also, blindly deleting any existing directory is destructive: a user's own incomplete/manual checkout in `vendor/MonkeyOCRv2` is removed without warning. Prefer cloning into a unique staging directory (`target.with_name(f"{target.name}.tmp-{os.getpid()}")`) and an atomic `os.replace`, guarded by a module-level `threading.Lock`.

content: The `try` here only guards decoding errors, but `_fernet()` is invoked inside it and raises `RuntimeError` when `TABULARIUM_VAULT_KEY` is not set or `cryptography` is missing. That exception escapes `get()`, so the documented "absent secret" contract (`""`) is broken, and `has()` propagates it too: e.g. `compute_profiles._out()` calls `vault.has(ref)` while serializing every profile, turning a listing into an HTTP 500 whenever the key is unconfigured (only `api/system.py` guards against `RuntimeError`). Either catch the configuration error here or make `has()` degrade to `False`.

Any string that is not a valid Fernet key is silently converted into a key with a single, unsalted SHA-256. Two problems: (1) a malformed/typo'd `TABULARIUM_VAULT_KEY` (e.g. value copied with quotes) never fails fast — secrets get written under an unintended derived key, `unreadable_names()` reports nothing while the typo is in place, and the data becomes unreadable the moment the key is corrected; (2) for a human passphrase this is a fast, unsalted KDF, so a low-entropy key can be brute-forced offline from a stolen `secrets` table. Validate strictly (reject keys that are not valid Fernet keys) or, if passphrases must be supported, derive with PBKDF2/scrypt and a documented salt/iteration count.

`get()` is documented/called as a lookup that returns `""` when the ref does not resolve to a readable secret, but a syntactically invalid ref (e.g. `"vault:"`, `"vault:  "`, or a ref with characters outside `_NAME`) raises `ValueError` out of it. Not every caller guards this: `api/cloud.py::_credential` passes an admin-supplied `credential_ref` straight to `vault.get()`, so a malformed ref yields a 500 instead of a 400/empty result. Return `""` for non-matching refs here (and keep `ValueError` only for `put()`/`delete()`, where the caller controls the name).

`normalize_username` never returns a falsy value: it raises `HTTPException(422)` when the name is shorter than 3 characters or contains disallowed characters. So the `or "utente"` fallback is dead code, and an OIDC user whose provider label is 1–2 chars (e.g. `preferred_username="ab"`, or a label that sanitizes down to 2 chars) fails the very first login with the `oidc_user` error instead of being provisioned. Validate/fallback explicitly instead of relying on a truthiness check.

content:
This reassigns `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` at module scope of the anyio library, from inside the request path, and never restores the original. Two problems:
1. The mutation is process-wide and permanent for the rest of the session, so any application code (or third-party lib such as httpx/anyio internals) that legitimately awaits `run_sync` to offload blocking work will silently execute it inline on the event loop instead — behaviour that does not match production and can deadlock/hang.
2. Patching on every request is redundant and hides ordering issues (the first request mutates global state for everything that runs afterwards, including other tests).

Apply the patch once (ideally via a `monkeypatch`-style fixture that restores it at teardown) instead of mutating the library attribute inside `_request`.

The application lifespan is entered and exited for every single request, whereas Starlette's `TestClient` runs it once for the `with TestClient(app) as client:` block. `app/main.py::lifespan` performs stateful work (`init_db()`, `live.hub.bind_loop(...)`, `reconcile_jobs()` for trainer/serve/recognition/benchmark/cloud/auto_training); running it per request means:
- reconciliation and DB initialization are executed N times per test, which can reorder/reset app state between requests of the same test (e.g. jobs started by the previous request);
- `live.hub.bind_loop()` keeps a reference to the loop that `asyncio.run` closes immediately after the request, so a later `hub.publish(...)` (via `call_soon_threadsafe`) targets a closed loop.

Enter the lifespan once (in `__enter__`) with a single long-lived loop, and close it in `__exit__`, rather than around each request.

`asyncio.run` creates and closes a fresh event loop per request and raises `RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop` if the client is ever used from async test code/plugin. Combined with the per-request lifespan above, every request gets a different loop, so anything cached with the loop (hub loop binding, threads, futures) is invalidated right after the response. Prefer a single persistent loop owned by the client instance (created in `__enter__`, shut down in `__close__`/`__exit__`) and reuse it for all requests.

Cookies are only ever added or overwritten; a `Set-Cookie` that deletes the cookie (`Max-Age=0`/`Expires` in the past, as sent by `/api/auth/logout`) leaves the stale entry in `self.cookies`, which keeps sending `cookie: tab_session=<old token>` on subsequent requests. Real `TestClient`/httpx removes such cookies. Since tests like `test_auth.py::test_logout_invalidates_session` rely on the real client's cookie semantics, this divergence can mask regressions. Remove the entry when the morsel expires or carries an empty value.

`stream()` performs a fully buffered request (`self.request(...)`) and yields the completed response, so the SSE tests (`test_prelabel.py` reading `response.iter_lines()`) never exercise incremental streaming: the whole body is materialised before the first line is consumed. That both hides streaming/latency bugs and buffers unbounded event streams in memory. Either use `AsyncClient.stream(...)` with a persistent loop so lines are produced lazily, or explicitly document that true streaming is not covered by this compatibility client.

Unknown constructor arguments are silently swallowed by `*args, **kwargs`. A test passing e.g. `raise_server_exceptions=False` or `backend=...` would be accepted but ignored, and `head()` (and `cookies`/`headers` property setters) are missing, so the tests would run against different semantics than Starlette's client without any signal. Consider consuming the known kwargs explicitly and raising `TypeError` for the rest, and add the missing `head()` helper.

The temporary root is created at import time and never removed, so every test session leaks a `tabularium-tests-*` directory (with a DB and any generated artifacts) into `/tmp`. Consider registering an `atexit`/session-scoped fixture finalizer that removes `_TMP_ROOT` (`shutil.rmtree(..., ignore_errors=True)`) when the DB handles are closed.
`config` is imported but never referenced anywhere in this script, so it is dead code (and it additionally forces the backend package import at module load). Remove the import.

Timeout wiring is inconsistent: the HTTP client is built with a timeout clamped to 5-30 s, while each `end2end` call receives `args.timeout` (default 300 s). `VllmClient._chat` uses `timeout=(10, self.timeout)` as the read timeout, so for non-streaming adapters (and for any token gap longer than 30 s while streaming) `requests` raises a read timeout long before the intended 300 s budget; the reported `wall_s`/failures then reflect the client clamp, not the value under test. `int()` also silently truncates fractional `--timeout` values. Use the same budget for the HTTP client, e.g. `timeout=int(args.timeout)`.
suggestion_code: client = inference.VllmClient(timeout=max(5, int(args.timeout)))

content: On the failure path `client.last_trace` / `client.last_text` are not reset per call: `VllmClient` only overwrites them inside `_chat` after a successful request. If `end2end` raises before any token is produced (pixel resizing, connection error, timeout on the first attempt) these attributes still hold the previous page/attempt values, so the failed entry gets another run's metrics and content head attached — misleading for a benchmark. Reset them (e.g. `client.last_trace = {}` / `client.last_text = ""`) before each attempt and report the values only when the current run actually produced them.

Catching every exception and returning `None` makes a genuine OTSL/HTML parse failure indistinguishable from a non-table item (both yield `table_shape: null`), so a regression in table parsing would look like "no tables on this page" in the benchmark output. Prefer letting the error propagate (the caller already wraps per-run failures) or return a distinct marker/diagnostic string that ends up in the report.

except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001
        return None
